Galatians is the most urgent letter ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ ever wrote. There are no warm thanks at the start and no greetings to friends at the end. Paul has heard that the churches he founded in ⟦l:galatia_431|Galatia⟧ are being persuaded to adopt a different message, and he writes in alarm, with anger and with deep affection, to call them back before it is too late.

To understand the letter we need to go back to the beginning of ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s missionary work, as Acts describes it. The church at ⟦l:antioch_68|Antioch⟧ in ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧, the first great centre of believers outside the Jewish homeland, sent out Paul and ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧ as missionaries. Barnabas, a Jewish believer from ⟦l:cyprus_316|Cyprus⟧, had been the first to vouch for Paul in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ after his conversion, and had brought him to Antioch to teach. The two men crossed to Cyprus and then travelled into the highlands of central ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧ Minor, in what is now Turkey. They preached in ⟦l:antioch_69|Pisidian Antioch⟧, ⟦l:iconium_590|Iconium⟧, ⟦l:lystra_742|Lystra⟧ and ⟦l:derbe_330|Derbe⟧, towns that lay within the Roman province of ⟦l:galatia_431|Galatia⟧. Wherever there was a synagogue they began there, and Gentiles as well as Jews believed. They also met fierce opposition. At Lystra Paul was stoned and left for dead. Paul himself recalls that he first came to the Galatians because of an illness, and that they welcomed him as if he were an angel of God.

These are the churches ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ is writing to. They were mainly Gentiles, people who had once worshipped the gods of their own towns and had turned to the God of Israel through faith in ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧.

After ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ left, other teachers arrived. Paul never names them, but the letter makes their message clear. They were Jewish believers in ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, and they insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, including its calendar of holy days, if they were truly to belong to the people of God. They also cast doubt on Paul himself, suggesting that he was a second-hand apostle, dependent on the leaders in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. Some of the Galatians were being persuaded.

This was not a small matter in the early church. The question of whether Gentile believers had to become Jews was argued in ⟦l:antioch_68|Antioch⟧, in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and wherever Jewish and Gentile believers met. Acts tells of a gathering of apostles and elders in Jerusalem called to settle it. Galatians was written in the heat of that argument.

For ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧, the issue went to the heart of the gospel. If Gentiles had to keep the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ to be accepted by God, then the death of Christ was not enough. He writes to defend both his message and his calling, and he does so in three movements. First he tells his own story: how he received the gospel by revelation from ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus Christ⟧, not from any human teacher, how his dealings with the apostles in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ confirmed it, and how he once confronted ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ himself at ⟦l:antioch_68|Antioch⟧. Then he argues from the Galatians' own experience of the Holy Spirit and from the Scriptures, returning again and again to ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧, the father of the Jewish people, who was counted righteous by faith centuries before the law was given. Finally he shows what the freedom he defends looks like in practice: not a licence to do as one pleases, but a life led by ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧, marked by love and by bearing one another's burdens. He closes with a few lines in his own large handwriting.

Many of the ideas ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ sets out here briefly and urgently he would later develop at greater length, and in a calmer tone, in his letter to the Romans.
1:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ opens with a description of himself that already signals the conflict at the heart of the letter. He is an apostle, sent not by any human authority but by ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus Christ⟧ and God the Father. His rivals in ⟦l:galatia_431|Galatia⟧ have questioned exactly that.

In almost every other letter, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ follows his greeting with a thanksgiving for his readers. Here he leaves it out and goes straight to his astonishment. The Galatians are so quickly deserting the one who called them and turning to a different gospel, which, Paul says, is no gospel at all. Twice he pronounces a curse on anyone who preaches another message, even an angel from heaven.

Then he begins to tell his own story. He was once a zealous persecutor of the church, advancing in Judaism beyond his contemporaries, until God revealed his Son to him. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s account of the years that followed is carefully chosen. He went to ⟦l:arabia_80|Arabia⟧ and back to ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧, he visited ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ only after three years, and even then he stayed just fifteen days with ⟦p:peter_2745|Cephas⟧, that is ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧, and met ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ the brother of the Lord. His point is that his gospel did not come from the leaders in Jerusalem.
2:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ continues his account of his own life. Fourteen years later, he says, he went up to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ again, with ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧, his partner on the first missionary journey, and with ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧, a Greek believer. What matters to Paul is the outcome. He set out his gospel before the leaders, and they added nothing to it. Titus was not required to be circumcised. ⟦p:james_719|James⟧, ⟦p:peter_2745|Cephas⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ recognised that Paul had been entrusted with the gospel to the Gentiles, and gave him and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship.

Then ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ tells of a moment when that agreement was put to the test. At ⟦l:antioch_68|Antioch⟧, ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ had been eating freely with Gentile believers. When certain men came from ⟦p:james_719|James⟧, Peter began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of the circumcision group, and the other Jewish believers followed, even ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧. Shared meals were at the centre of the early church's life, and to separate at table was to say that Gentile believers were not fully part of God's people.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ confronted ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ publicly. His account of what he said leads directly into the central claim of the letter: a person is justified not by works of the law, but by faith in ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus Christ⟧.
3:
With his own story told, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ now turns to the Galatians themselves, and he begins with a rebuke. O foolish Galatians, he writes, who has bewitched you? When he first preached among them, Christ crucified was portrayed before their very eyes.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ appeals to their own experience. They received the Holy Spirit, and saw God work miracles among them, by believing what they heard, not by keeping the law. Why would they now try to complete by human effort what God began by his Spirit?

Then ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ turns to Scripture, and above all to ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧, whom the teachers in ⟦l:galatia_431|Galatia⟧ would surely claim as their own. Paul goes back to the word in Genesis: Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him, and that promise came four hundred and thirty years before the law was given at ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧. Paul then asks what the law was for, and he compares it to a guardian who supervised a child until the child came of age. The chapter ends with a famous description of the new community in Christ, where there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.
4:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has just compared the law to a guardian, and the Galatians to heirs who have now come of age. He develops that picture here. In the ancient world an heir who was still a child had no more freedom than a slave, until the time set by his father. When the time had fully come, Paul says, God sent his Son to redeem those under the law, and sent his Spirit into their hearts, so that they cry Abba, Father.

Then he asks why, having come to know God, the Galatians want to go back to slavery. Before their conversion they served gods that were no gods. Now they are beginning to observe special days and seasons, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ treats this as a return to the same bondage.

In the middle of the chapter ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s tone becomes intensely personal. He reminds them how he first came to them, ill, and how warmly they received him. He calls them his children, and pictures himself in the pains of childbirth again until Christ is formed in them. The chapter ends with an illustration drawn from Genesis, the story of ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧'s two sons, Ishmael born to the slave woman ⟦p:hagar_1348|Hagar⟧ and ⟦p:isaac_616|Isaac⟧ born to the free woman ⟦p:sarah_2473|Sarah⟧, which Paul reads as a picture of two covenants.
5:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has finished his argument from ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧'s two sons, and he states its conclusion in a single sentence: it is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Now he spells out what is at stake in practical terms.

If the Galatian men accept circumcision as a requirement for belonging to God's people, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ warns, they commit themselves to keeping the whole law, and Christ will be of no benefit to them. He speaks with unusual sharpness about the teachers who are unsettling them. And if anyone says that Paul himself still preaches circumcision, he has one answer: then why is he still being persecuted?

Then the chapter turns. Freedom from the law, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ insists, is not freedom to indulge the flesh. It is freedom to serve one another in love, which fulfils the whole law. If instead they go on biting and devouring one another, Paul warns, they will be consumed by one another. Then he sets two ways of living side by side, at war with each other: the acts of the flesh, and the fruit of ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧, in a short list that has become one of the best known passages in his letters.
6:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has described life led by ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧, and in his final chapter he brings it down to the life of a congregation. If someone is caught in wrongdoing, those who are spiritual are to restore him gently, watching themselves as they do. They are to carry one another's burdens, share good things with those who teach them, and not grow weary in doing good. Paul reaches for the farmer's picture of sowing and reaping, which his readers in an agricultural region would have known well.

Then ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ writes the closing lines in his own hand. Letters in his world were usually written out by a secretary, and Paul did this in several of his letters as a personal mark. Here he draws attention to the large letters he is using. He does not say why.

In these last lines he returns one final time to the teachers who are pressing circumcision on the Galatians. He accuses them of wanting to make a good impression and to avoid persecution. For his own part he will boast only in the cross of Christ. What counts, he says, is neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. He ends by saying that he bears on his body the marks of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, the scars of the beatings and the stoning he had suffered.
